headline: Bay water hits 79°F and pushes the fluke straight to the inlet
subhead: Great South Bay is too warm for its own good this week, so the doormats and the smart anglers are both heading for Fire Island Inlet.
body_markdown:
Last week the bay basically turned into bathwater. I ran a thermometer off the transom out past the Nicoll Bay flats on Thursday and it read pushing 79 degrees on the surface — that's summer-camp-pool warm, not fluke-holding warm. We had a stretch of light southerly wind that just sat on the water for days, no mixing, no relief, and it cooked the shallow flats and the channels off Sayville and Patchogue into soup. Fluke don't like that. Neither do the bass, honestly. So the fish did what smart fish do — they left.

What's coming this week changes the equation a little. We're building toward a new moon on the 13th, and that means spring tides are stacking up — bigger swings, stronger current, more water moving through Fire Island Inlet on both the flood and the drain. That's the best thing that could happen for us right now. Stronger current means more exchange between that overheated bay water and the cooler, cleaner stuff coming in off the ocean side, which the analyst data has been showing running around 71 degrees where the upwelling's been working the beach. When that cold water gets pulled through the inlet on the outgoing, it drags bait and predators with it, and it gives the fluke and the bass a reason to stack up right where the funnel narrows. Watch for that current to really turn on Friday through Monday as the new moon tightens its grip — that's your window.

So here's what's actually happening on the water. The fluke bite in the open bay has gone soft — guys drifting the flats off West Sayville and the Nicoll Bay channel are picking at short fish and losing patience fast. But move to the inlet itself, anywhere from the Democrat Point side down through the Robert Moses bridges, and it's a different story. I had a solid morning last outgoing tide working 25 to 35 feet just west of the second bridge span with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail teased with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet in pearl white, dragging it slow along bottom on the drift. Picked up two keepers in the 4-to-5-pound class and lost what felt like a bigger fish right at the boat. The pattern is consistent — fluke are stacking on the edges of the channel where that cooler ocean water is pushing in against the warmer bay flow, and the outgoing tide two hours either side of dead low has been the most productive window. If you're not marking bait on the sonar down around 20-30 feet near the bridge piers, keep moving — they're bunched up tight this week, not spread thin.

Striper action is a night game right now, which is normal for July but worth saying plainly — daytime bass fishing in the heat has been mostly a bust. Guys working bunker chunks off Democrat Point after dark on the last two hours of the incoming have been connecting with fish in the mid-20s to low 30-inch range, some better mixed in. If you want a shot at something bigger, fish the sandbar drop right off the point where the current rips hardest on that new moon flood — that's where the bait gets pinned and the bigger fish sit in the wash waiting. Live eels fished on a fish-finder rig, or just chunked bunker on a fireball rig, both been working. Don't bother during the day unless there's real cloud cover and a stiff breeze breaking up the surface.

Bluefish have been the reliable player this week when everything else got moody. Bunker schools pushing through the inlet on the tide changes have chopper blues in the 3-to-6-pound range busting bait right on the surface, especially around sunrise off the south side of the Fire Island Lighthouse rip. Metal — Kastmasters, Hopkins, anything silver you can rip through the surface — will get bit fast. It's not subtle fishing, but it's fun, and it's about the only guaranteed action if the fluke and bass are being difficult.

I want to be straight with you about weakfish — they're basically not happening. Water's warm enough, has been for weeks, and there's just nothing showing up in the bay or off the inlet. I know some of you remember when the weakfish run here was a real event; this isn't that year. I'd stop planning trips around them until something changes.

Porgies are a modest bright spot for the bay-bound crowd — light action over the reef structure off Sayville and around the Robert Moses causeway rocks, small pieces of clam on a hi-lo rig taking a mix of decent-sized scup, nothing spectacular but steady if you need a bucket of fish for dinner without fighting the inlet current.

One more thing worth watching — there's chatter about bonito and Spanish mackerel starting to show on the ocean side of the eastern inlets this week, riding that same warm push that's been moving west along the south shore. Nothing confirmed at Fire Island yet, but if that pattern keeps sliding our way, Democrat Point and the outer bar could see the first fish of the year sooner than usual. Worth keeping a rod rigged with small metal on the ready if you're out there working bass or blues.

Looking ahead, I'd put my time at the inlet through the weekend. The new moon spring tides building into Monday should sharpen up that current exchange and keep pulling fluke and bait through the bridges — that's where I'm starting every trip. If the wind stays reasonable, the outgoing tide Friday through Sunday morning is the play. Plan B if the inlet gets crowded or the current's too ripping to hold bottom — work the porgy grounds off Sayville for something to show for the day.
